argument: Introducing Keiji Nishitani of the Kyoto School, the episode argues that just as people can fake a relationship with death, most people never truly encounter nihilism. Western thought, smuggling in monotheistic and Platonic assumptions that a moral order and stable essences should be given, treats missing meaning as an emergency and responds positively, trying to solve nihilism by willing new values through the self, as Nietzsche did. Nishitani instead treats nihilism as a lived experiment each particular self must run, one that, pressed into the Great Doubt, turns its questioning on the questioner and finds no fixed essence at the bottom of the self, only no-thing-ness and meaning gained through changing relations, like a word in a linguistic network rather than a wave merging with the ocean. Lived this way, nihilism overcomes itself and opens onto sunyata, an emptiness that is not a void but a denial of fixed, independent existence, an immanent aspect of this reality accessed in the here and now.
keyIdeas: Just as you can have a merely theoretical relationship with death, you can claim to face nihilism without ever really encountering it; the person who says life is meaningless and just seeks comfort is actually choosing comfort and security as values.

The classic western response treats nihilism as a problem to be solved by creating meaning through the self and the will, because western thought smuggles in monotheistic assumptions that a moral order should be given from outside.

Defining nihilism through historical examples or as a static feeling of despair leaves out its crucial dimension as a subjective experiment each particular self must run for itself, which can lead through the Great Doubt.

Questioning the questioner reveals that at the bottom of the self is no-thing-ness: no fixed essence, only meaning gained through constantly changing relations, better modeled by how word meanings work in structural linguistics than by a wave realizing it is the ocean.

Sunyata or emptiness is not a void or a claim that nothing exists but a denial of fixed, independent existence; it is an immanent aspect of this reality accessed in the here and now, and nihilism truly lived eventually overcomes itself.

terms.def: The movement of thinkers out of Kyoto, Japan, including Nishitani, who radically engaged with western ideas like existentialism, though fans resist reducing it to an east-meets-west blend.
The Zen Buddhist name for the transformative period opened when nihilistic questioning is steered into rather than solved, revealing how deep the well of nihilism goes.
The Mahayana Buddhist concept that nothing is independent, self-causing, or self-sustaining with an essence; everything is a thing only through what it relates to and depends on.
Emptiness: not a void or a claim that nothing exists, but the denial that things have fixed, independent existence, an immanent aspect of this reality that is our birthright.
Nishitani's term for nihilism understood as an immanent aspect of being itself, something to embrace and learn to be with rather than a problem to run from.

a sort of POSITIVE response to Nihilism…that’s a CLASSIC kind of response that comes out of a western style of thinking. The idea is: that Nihilism…is a problem to be SOLVED.
it is FILLED with people making very MONOTHEISTIC, ABRAHAMIC assumptions… that there’s SUPPOSED TO BE a moral order to the world, that’s GIVEN to us from the outside by a supernatural God.
it will always IGNORE an entire piece of what people are even TALKING about when they DESCRIBE Nihilism: the subjective, LIVED experience of Nihilism…TO a particular SELF that is grappling with it.

this FEELING they’re having…is actually EVIDENCE of the fact… that they’re someone who’s QUESTIONING their reality beyond the conventions they were born into.
